reasons: [coverage/major] D1 [criteriaAssessments C6; tradeoffs; alternatives (full rollout and do-not-proceed); CL7, CL10] The draft never asks whether the 32-hour week keeps full pay or cuts pay pro rata, and it does not ask what pay terms applied in Nordvik, Varmland or the UK pilot. That one question decides the cost case under C6 and how well the benefits transfer. At full pay, cost per paid hour rises 25% (40/32). That is the main cost line, bigger than the overtime and backfill scenarios the draft models: K7's 375 FTE at full pay means about 25% more payroll. At reduced pay, Nordvik's wellbeing and attrition effects (E4) may not carry over at all, because the source does not say the trial arms had the same pay. The draft also leaves out contract, benefits, employee-consultation and legal implementation issues, which matter for a 300-person Q2 change.

[evidence_sufficiency/major] D2 [verdict ('Two benefits look real'); alternatives 'Do not proceed'; C4 assessment ('Wellbeing improves'); CL5, CL6] The verdict says 'Two benefits look real', and the do-not-proceed alternative cites 'a validated burnout improvement and a possible 30% relative attrition reduction'. The supplied source (source-B) gives no CI, p-value or significance test for either result. It does not label the 9.1% and 13.0% arms. It also does not say whether the 0.4 SD burnout improvement is a difference between arms or a before-and-after change within the treatment arm. The draft notes the unlabelled arms under C5, but it does not flag the before-and-after vs between-arm ambiguity for wellbeing. In this sample, a 3.9-point attrition gap over 9 months, annualised, could easily be non-significant. 'Validated' describes the scale, not the finding, but the alternatives section reads it as a validated effect. Nordvik's existence also cannot be verified (E8). On this evidence, 'look real' overstates what is known. These benefits are the draft's main reason for rejecting 'do not proceed'.

[reasoning_validity/major] D3 [verdict; C2 assessment and strengths; CL2; CL10/K8] The draft calls output 'roughly flat on 20% fewer hours' as if it were established. Two problems. (a) The 20% cut is an assumption: source-B does not state baseline hours, a point the draft itself makes in E5 and C2 but drops from the verdict. (b) The -2% is pooled across 112 teams, including non-support 'billable output'. The customer-service subgroup output is not reported. For a coverage-bound support org, the lower CI bound of -7% is material: about 21 FTE-equivalents of throughput at 300 staff. The subgroup's own +11% first-response penalty suggests support may sit at the worse end of the range. C2's strength that 'the CI excludes large losses' treats the pooled interval as if it applied to support. K8 (306 staff) builds on this by assuming the pooled per-hour gain carries over to support, which E3 calls into question.

[decision_usefulness/major] D4 [verdict; alternatives 'Staggered, measured pilot'; practicalImplications] The recommended pilot ('2 to 4 teams for 3 to 6 months') does not fit the outcomes it is meant to test, and the draft has no decision rules. Assume roughly 10 to 30 agents in the pilot, at 9 to 13% annual attrition. A 3 to 6 month window would produce only a handful of leavers, so the attrition effect, which the draft treats as a main benefit, cannot be detected. The draft concedes 'attrition effects need longer' but does not resize the pilot. It also gives no go/no-go or scale-up thresholds, for example an acceptable change in first-response time or SLA, or an overtime ceiling. It says nothing on timing relative to Q2, on how pilot teams would be chosen (volunteer teams bring back selection and Hawthorne bias), or on what happens after the pilot. 'Stop rules in advance' is stated, but no rules are given.

[decision_usefulness/major] D1 [alternatives 'Randomised, staggered pilot'; practicalImplications (selection, go/no-go rules); CL14] The resized pilot (about 60 agents in randomly assigned teams vs about 60 in control, at least 6 months) gets a power check for attrition (K16, K17) but none for the metrics that actually gate the decision. At typical support team sizes, 60 agents is only about 5 to 8 teams per arm. Nordvik needed 112 randomised teams to get a total-output CI of about +/-5 points. A cluster-randomised comparison with about 6 teams per arm would have a much wider interval, so 'tickets resolved per team ... materially worse than control' and first-response-time differences of the size Nordvik reports (+11%, CI +4% to +18%) may not be distinguishable from noise. The draft correctly concludes that attrition cannot gate the decision, but it does not apply the same reasoning to throughput and FRT. Either the pilot is underpowered for its own go/no-go rules, or the analysis needs a stated design (for example, weekly difference-in-differences with pre-period baselines, or more or smaller clusters). This material is new in draft 2.

findings: [minor/reviewer] D1 [CL15; K19; verdict (pilot detectability sentence); alternatives 'Randomised, staggered pilot'] The K19/CL15 detectability check is new in draft 3 and uses the wrong benchmark effect. Source-B reports the +11% first-response penalty (CI +4% to +18%) only for customer-service teams on non-staggered schedules ('unless staggered schedules used'). The recommended pilot is staggered by design. So the effect it has to detect is the unreported staggered effect, which is presumably smaller, not +11%. CL15's line 'a first-response effect of Nordvik's size (+11%) would be barely distinguishable from zero' therefore overstates what the pilot can show on response time. The scaling also assumes all 31 customer-service teams sit behind that CI. If the 'unless staggered' figure comes from a non-staggered subset of those teams, the per-team variance and the scaled half-width change as well. The draft calls the scaling rough, but it should say plainly that a staggered pilot is mostly unable to detect a realistic staggered first-response effect, and that its value on response time lies in the SLA safety thresholds. K18 = 5*sqrt(112/12) = 15.28 and K19 = 7*sqrt(31/12) = 11.25 are both arithmetically correct.

[minor/reviewer] D3 [verdict (full-pay cost sentences)] The rewritten verdict cost sentence says 'The real cost is losing 20% of agent-hours (K5)' and quotes 375 FTE to hold hours constant (K7). It does not mention that, on Nordvik's pooled estimate, output per hour rises, so the loss of agent-hours does not translate one-for-one into lost throughput. C6 and CL10 give the 306 optimistic bound (K8). With only the 375 figure, a reader of the verdict could take 75 extra FTE as the expected buy-back need rather than an upper bound. One clause in the verdict giving the 306 to 375 range, with its caveats, would fix this.

[minor/reviewer] D2 [practicalImplications (Selection and design); alternatives 'Randomised, staggered pilot'] The new pilot design says to randomise 'the smallest units that can be rostered independently (for example pods rather than whole teams)' 'within comparable queues' in order to get more clusters. First-response time and SLA attainment are usually queue-level measures. If pilot and control pods serve the same queue, they share one first-response figure, so randomising pods adds no independent first-response observations and builds in contamination. The draft notes that contamination 'rises as clusters get smaller' but does not say that the randomised unit must own its queue or channel, or else have its first-response time attributed per agent, for the extra-clusters fix to work on response time. As written, the main remedy for the power problem may not work for the metric that matters most.
